preamble: Rounding and raising of the open back vowel [ɑ(ː)] to open-mid [ɔ(ː)]. In southern and Midland Middle English, Old English long ā /ɑː/ became /ɔː/ (hām > hom, bān > bon, āc > ok), while Northern Middle English fronted it to /aː/ instead; the new /ɔː/ was later raised to /oː/ in the Great Vowel Shift. Much earlier, in the prehistory of Proto-Germanic, the long /ɑː/ that resulted from the merger of PIE *ā and *ō was rounded to /ɔː/ (*swātuz > *swōtuz 'sweet', *dāmaz > *dōmaz 'judgement').

examples.note: Wiktionary gives early Middle English /hɑːm/, /bɑːn/, /ɑːk/ (the Old English vowel unchanged) and Northern /haːm/, /baːn/, /aːk/, where the rounding did not take place. The new /ɔː/ was later raised to /oː/ in the Great Vowel Shift.
PIE long *ō and *ā first merged as /ɑː/, which was then rounded to /ɔː/; the overlong vowel followed the same path (*-âz > *-ôz).

sources: Wikipedia contributors (2026). Phonological history of English open back vowels. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonological_history_of_English_open_back_vowels
